extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and policymakers concerned with the French Revolution (late-18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political essay arguing against revolutionary doctrine and practice in France, defending constitutional experience and cautioning against metaphysical claims of absolute rights. It addresses legitimacy, prudence, and the moral consequences of revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of absolute 'rights of men'
rubrics_metrics.description: The pretended 'rights of men' admit no temperament and no compromise: anything withheld from their full demand is so much of fraud and injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of absolute natural rights with suspicion: if asserted without limits they undermine prescription, compromise, and the security of government. Evaluate political claims for their practicability and effects on existing institutions rather than for metaphysical purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for historical constitutions and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The merits of a constitution are confirmed by the solid test of long experience and an increasing public strength and national prosperity; it is with infinite caution that any man ought to venture upon pulling down an edifice which has answered in any tolerable degree for ages the common purposes of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to precedent, long practice, and proven institutions. Avoid radical overhaul of constitutional arrangements absent reliable models of approved utility and long experience demonstrating improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government as a practical instrument for human wants
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is a contrivance of human wisdom to provide for human wants. Men have a right that these wants should be provided for by this wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge governments by how well they secure practical goods: justice between fellows, protection of industry and its fruits, support for offspring, instruction, and consolation in death. Rights include access to these provisions rather than abstract entitlements divorced from implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man should be judge in his own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first motives to civil society... is, that no man should be judge in his own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil society requires institutions that remove adjudication from self-interest. Evaluate proposals and institutional designs on whether they secure impartial adjudication and restrain private passions that would otherwise dominate judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights must be limited by social convention
rubrics_metrics.description: If civil society be the offspring of convention, that convention must be its law... how can any man claim, under the conventions of civil society, rights which do not so much as suppose its existence,--rights which are absolutely repugnant to it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rights claims for compatibility with the conventions and structures that enable civil society; eliminate or modify purported rights that are incompatible with collective governance and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints are part of the rights framework
rubrics_metrics.description: In this sense the restraints on men, as well as their liberties, are to be reckoned among their rights. But as the liberties and the restrictions vary with times and circumstances, and admit of infinite modifications, they cannot be settled upon any abstract rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating liberty, recognize that lawful restraints are themselves protective rights. Avoid abstract, one-size-fits-all rules; tailor liberties and restrictions to historical circumstances and practical needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design requires experience and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of constructing a commonwealth... is, like every other experimental science, not to be taught a priori... it is with infinite caution that any man ought to venture upon pulling down an edifice which has answered in any tolerable degree for ages the common purposes of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach constitutional reform as an empirical, experience-driven task. Favor complex, tested arrangements over simplistic contrivances; beware designers who promise simple solutions to complex social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political moderation and compromise over extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of men are in a sort of middle, incapable of definition, but not impossible to be discerned... these are often in balances between differences of good,--in compromises sometimes between good and evil, and sometimes between evil and evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value middle-ground solutions and compromises; evaluate proposals by their capacity to balance competing goods rather than by adherence to extreme or absolute principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish moral right from sheer power
rubrics_metrics.description: By these theorists the right of the people is almost always sophistically confounded with their power... Men have no right to what is not reasonable, and to what is not for their benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate popular power or capability with legitimate moral right. Scrutinize whether a claimed entitlement is reasonable and beneficial rather than simply backed by force or majoritarian capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid habitual rhetoric of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: This continual talk of resistance and revolution... renders the habit of society dangerously valetudinary; it is taking periodical doses of mercury sublimate... This distemper of remedy, grown habitual, relaxes and wears out, by a vulgar and prostituted use, the spring of that spirit which is to be exerted on great occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize recurring revolutionary rhetoric and ceremonial agitation as corrosive to effective civic virtue and prudence. Reserve radical measures for genuine emergencies to preserve moral seriousness and efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of triumphalizing violence and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: I find a preacher of the Gospel profaning the beautiful and prophetic ejaculation... and applying it... to the most horrid, atrocious, and afflicting spectacle... 'leading in triumph'... must shock the moral taste of every well-born mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject celebratory or religious framing of massacres, assassinations, and cruel spectacles. Evaluate political actions by their moral character; do not permit public recognition that glorifies brutality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy requires freedom from coercion and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is notorious that all their measures are decided before they are debated... under the terror of the bayonet, and the lamp-post, and the torch to their houses, they are obliged to adopt all the crude and desperate measures suggested by clubs...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the legitimacy of representative bodies by their independence from coercion, free deliberation, and absence of mob or military intimidation. Decisions made under fear or external dominance lack genuine authority.
